title: Πικρὸς ὀϊστός
about: Athena goes down into the Trojan ranks in the likeness of Laodocus, a son of Antenor, and finds Pandarus standing among the troops he has led from the Aesepus. She urges him to shoot Menelaus, promising thanks and glory from all the Trojans and above all from Alexander, and tells him to vow a hecatomb to Apollo; the senseless man is persuaded. He strings the bow made from the horns of a wild goat he once shot himself, has his companions hold up their shields to screen him, and looses an arrow. Athena turns it aside as a mother brushes a fly from her sleeping child and steers it to the join of belt and breastplate. It passes through belt, breastplate and belly-guard but only grazes the skin, and the blood runs down Menelaus’ legs like crimson dye on ivory. Agamemnon and Menelaus shudder; Menelaus is relieved to see the barbs outside the wound, and Agamemnon, holding his brother’s hand, laments the broken oaths, foretells the fall of Troy, and says how shamed he would be to go home if Menelaus died.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκεν Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε.
sentences.l: So then someone of the Achaeans and of the Trojans kept saying.
sentences.i: So some man, Achaean or Trojan, would say.
sentences.n: This line is the narrator’s tag on the onlookers’ speech that ended the last part, so the narrator is back in charge. τις ‘someone’ stands for each watcher in turn. εἴπεσκεν is an iterative imperfect of εἶπον, ‘would say, kept saying’; the -σκ- marks repetition, as in εἴπεσκεν at 81. Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε is a genitive saying which side each speaker belongs to. After the paragraph break the story turns from the onlookers to what Athena does next.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἀνδρὶ ἰκέλη Τρώων κατεδύσεθ’ ὅμιλον
Λαοδόκῳ Ἀντηνορίδῃ κρατερῷ αἰχμητῇ,
sentences.l:
And she, like a man, went down into the throng of the Trojans,
Laodocus, Antenor’s-son, a strong spearman,
sentences.i: And she went down into the Trojan throng in the likeness of a man, Laodocus, son of Antenor, a strong spearman,
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Athena, who darted to earth at 78. She goes disguised: ἰκέλη ‘like’ takes the dative ἀνδρί ‘a man’, and Λαοδόκῳ names the man, in apposition, as a dative too. Ἀντηνορίδῃ is a patronymic, ‘Antenor’s-son’, and κρατερῷ αἰχμητῇ ‘strong spearman’ is a stock phrase for a warrior. κατεδύσεθ’ is an aorist with the epic -σε- in the stem, as in ἀνεδύσετο at 1.496: ‘went down into’ a crowd.

sentences.t: Πάνδαρον ἀντίθεον διζημένη εἴ που ἐφεύροι.
sentences.l: seeking godlike Pandarus, if somewhere she might find him.
sentences.i: She was looking for godlike Pandarus, in case she might find him somewhere.
sentences.n: Πάνδαρον is Pandarus, the archer from Zeleia already named in the Catalogue (2.827); the next line gives his father. ἀντίθεον ‘godlike’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. διζημένη is a participle ‘seeking’. εἴ που ἐφεύροι is an optative, ‘if somewhere she might find’: the optative says that finding him is her hope, not yet a fact, and που ‘somewhere’ shows she does not know where he stands.

sentences.t:
εὗρε Λυκάονος υἱὸν ἀμύμονά τε κρατερόν τε
ἑσταότ’·
sentences.l:
She found the son of Lycaon, both blameless and strong,
standing;
sentences.i: She found him, the blameless and strong son of Lycaon, standing there;
sentences.n: εὗρε is the aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, answering ἐφεύροι in 88. Λυκάονος υἱόν ‘son of Lycaon’ is Pandarus, now named by his father. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ and κρατερόν ‘strong’ are stock praise, and τε … τε means ‘both … and’. ἑσταότ’ is the elided perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, agreeing with υἱόν. The unit stops at the high point mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν κρατεραὶ στίχες ἀσπιστάων
λαῶν, οἵ οἱ ἕποντο ἀπ’ Αἰσήποιο ῥοάων·
sentences.l:
and about him the strong ranks of shield-bearing
people, who followed him from the streams of the Aesepus;
sentences.i: and around him were the strong ranks of his shield-bearing troops, who had followed him from the streams of the Aesepus;
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb of its own: ἀμφί … μιν ‘around him’ and the ranks are set beside him, and ‘were’ is added in the English. στίχες are ‘ranks’, rows of a battle line; ἀσπιστάων is the epic genitive plural of ἀσπιστής ‘shield-bearer’, and λαῶν ‘of the troops’ stands in apposition. οἵ οἱ ἕποντο: the first οἵ is ‘who’, the second οἱ is ‘him’ (dative), and ἕποντο ‘followed’ has no augment. Αἰσήποιο is the genitive of Αἴσηπος, a river.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words she spoke to him:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱσταμένη ‘standing’ (feminine, so still Athena) set the scene for the speech. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’; the Greek leaves out the person spoken to, and ‘to him’ is Pandarus. ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase of speech introduction and is translated every time: the image is of words that fly from speaker to hearer.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥά νύ μοί τι πίθοιο Λυκάονος υἱὲ δαΐφρον.
sentences.l: “Truly now, you might obey me in something, wise-minded son of Lycaon.
sentences.i: “Surely you might listen to me in something, wise-hearted son of Lycaon.
sentences.n: Athena opens by asking for his obedience. ἦ ῥά νύ is a run of particles, ‘truly now’, that begins a probing request. πίθοιο is an optative of πείθομαι ‘obey, listen to’, with the dative μοί ‘to me’ and τι ‘in something’. The edition ends with a full stop, and the English keeps a statement of what he might do, the proposal following in the next lines; ἦ ῥά νύ … could also open a question, ‘would you obey me …?’. Λυκάονος υἱέ is a vocative, ‘son of Lycaon’. δαΐφρον is the stock epithet of unsure sense: ‘wise-minded’ is the traditional reading, ‘warlike’ the other.

sentences.t:
τλαίης κεν Μενελάῳ ἐπιπροέμεν ταχὺν ἰόν,
πᾶσι δέ κε Τρώεσσι χάριν καὶ κῦδος ἄροιο,
ἐκ πάντων δὲ μάλιστα Ἀλεξάνδρῳ βασιλῆϊ.
sentences.l:
You would dare to send forth a swift arrow at Menelaus,
and with all the Trojans thanks and glory you would win,
and out of all, most of all, with Alexander the king.
sentences.i: You would dare to send a swift arrow at Menelaus, and you would win thanks and glory from all the Trojans, and most of all from king Alexander.
sentences.n: Athena offers a reward. τλαίης κεν and ἄροιο are optatives with κεν, ‘you would …’, the softened form of a proposal. τλαίης is from τλάω ‘dare’; ἐπιπροέμεν is an aorist infinitive, ‘to send forth at’; ἰόν is ‘arrow’. χάριν ‘thanks’ and κῦδος ‘glory’ are what Pandarus would win, ἄροιο from ἄρνυμαι ‘win’. Ἀλεξάνδρῳ βασιλῆϊ is ‘Alexander the king’: Alexander is the other name of Paris, the man whose quarrel with Menelaus started the war.

sentences.t: τοῦ κεν δὴ πάμπρωτα παρ’ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα φέροιο,
sentences.l: From him, indeed, before all others, splendid gifts you would carry off,
sentences.i: From him, first of all, you would carry off splendid gifts,
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘from him’ is Alexander, named at the end of 96, and παρ’ ‘from beside’ goes with it, or with φέροιο, though the words stand apart; either way the sense is ‘carry off from him’. πάμπρωτα is ‘first of all’, a neuter plural used as an adverb. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα ‘splendid gifts’ is the object of φέροιο, an optative with κεν, ‘you would carry off’. δή adds ‘indeed, surely’. The condition for the gift comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αἴ κεν ἴδῃ Μενέλαον ἀρήϊον Ἀτρέος υἱὸν
σῷ βέλεϊ δμηθέντα πυρῆς ἐπιβάντ’ ἀλεγεινῆς.
sentences.l:
if he should see Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus,
subdued by your shaft, having gone up on the grievous pyre.
sentences.i: if he sees Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus, overcome by your shaft and gone up on the grievous pyre.
sentences.n: αἴ κεν is the epic form of εἰ κεν, ‘if ever’, with the aorist subjunctive ἴδῃ ‘should see’; the subject is Alexander. Μενέλαον is the object, and Ἀτρέος υἱόν ‘son of Atreus’ with ἀρήϊον ‘warlike’ (stock epithet) says which son. δμηθέντα is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’; ἐπιβάντ’ is ‘having gone up on’, so the dead man is imagined laid on his funeral fire. βέλεϊ is the dative of βέλος ‘shaft’, σῷ ‘your’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ὀΐστευσον Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο,
sentences.l: But come, shoot an arrow at Menelaus the glorious,
sentences.i: But come, shoot at glorious Menelaus,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ‘but come’ turns from the reward to the request. ὀΐστευσον is an aorist imperative of ὀϊστεύω ‘shoot an arrow’, built on ὀϊστός ‘arrow’, and it takes the genitive of its target, Μενελάου. κυδαλίμοιο is the epic genitive of κυδάλιμος ‘glorious’, a stock epithet that is translated every time; the Odyssey gives it to the same man.

sentences.t:
εὔχεο δ’ Ἀπόλλωνι Λυκηγενέϊ κλυτοτόξῳ
ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων ῥέξειν κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην
οἴκαδε νοστήσας ἱερῆς εἰς ἄστυ Ζελείης.
sentences.l:
and pray to Apollo, Lycia-born, famed for the bow,
that of first-born lambs you will sacrifice a famous hecatomb
when you have come home to the city of sacred Zeleia.”
sentences.i: And pray to Apollo, the Lycia-born, famed for the bow, that you will sacrifice a famous hecatomb of first-born lambs when you have come home to the city of sacred Zeleia.”
sentences.n: Athena ends by telling him what to pray for. εὔχεο is a present imperative of εὔχομαι ‘pray’, and the prayer carries a promise: ῥέξειν is a future infinitive, ‘that you will sacrifice’. Λυκηγενέϊ is an epithet of Apollo whose sense is not certain; ‘born in Lycia’ is the usual explanation, and ‘wolf-born’ and ‘light-born’ have been proposed. κλυτοτόξῳ is ‘famed for the bow’. A hecatomb is properly a sacrifice of a hundred oxen, though here the victims are lambs. Ζελείης is Zeleia, Pandarus’ home town.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτ’ Ἀθηναίη, τῷ δὲ φρένας ἄφρονι πεῖθεν·
sentences.l: So spoke Athena, and the wits of him, senseless, she was persuading;
sentences.i: So Athena spoke, and she persuaded the wits of the senseless man.
sentences.n: The speech is over, and the poet comments at once. ὣς φάτ’ is ‘so spoke’ (φάτο with its last vowel dropped). τῷ … ἄφρονι is a dative, ‘for him, senseless’, naming the man whose φρένας ‘wits’ are the object; ἄφρων ‘senseless’ is a judgement of the narrator, who knows the plan will wreck the truce. πεῖθεν is the imperfect of πείθω ‘persuade’ without augment, ‘was persuading’; it shows the persuasion working, as the next lines show him act.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἐσύλα τόξον ἐΰξοον ἰξάλου αἰγὸς
ἀγρίου,
sentences.l:
At once he stripped the well-polished bow of a bounding
wild goat,
sentences.i: At once he bared the well-polished bow of a bounding wild goat,
sentences.n: ἐσύλα is the imperfect of συλάω ‘strip off, take off’; with τόξον ‘bow’ as its object the sense is taking the bow out of its covering, so ‘bared’ in the English. The same verb takes the lid off the quiver at 116. ἐΰξοον ‘well-polished’ is of uncertain formation. ἰξάλου ‘bounding’ is the usual explanation of a rare word, and its sense is not certain. The genitive ‘of a wild goat’ says what the bow is made of, which the next lines explain.

sentences.t:
ὅν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ στέρνοιο τυχήσας
πέτρης ἐκβαίνοντα δεδεγμένος ἐν προδοκῇσι
βεβλήκει πρὸς στῆθος·
sentences.i: That goat he had once hit himself, lying in wait for it in ambush as it came out from a rock, beneath the breast — he had struck it in the chest;
sentences.n: ὅν ‘which’ is the goat, object of βεβλήκει ‘had struck’ (a pluperfect). Two participles describe the shot: τυχήσας, from τυγχάνω ‘hit the mark’ (with ὑπὸ στέρνοιο ‘beneath the breast’), and δεδεγμένος, from δέχομαι, here ‘waiting for’. πέτρης ἐκβαίνοντα is ‘as it came out from a rock’. προδοκῇσι is a plural, ‘places of ambush’. The high point after στῆθος ‘chest’ is a pause before the goat’s fall.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἔμπεσε πέτρῃ.
sentences.l: and it fell on its back upon the rock.
sentences.i: and it fell on its back on the rock.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and it’ is the goat again, now the subject. ὕπτιος ‘on its back’ agrees with ὃ. ἔμπεσε is ἐν + ἔπεσε, ‘fell upon’, and the dative πέτρῃ ‘upon the rock’ is the same word as πέτρης in 107: the animal falls back upon the rock. The goat is dead, and from here the story is how its horns became a bow.

sentences.t: τοῦ κέρα ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἑκκαιδεκάδωρα πεφύκει·
sentences.l: Of it, the horns from its head, sixteen-palm-long, had grown;
sentences.i: The horns that had grown from its head were sixteen palms long;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of it’ is the goat; the genitive goes with κέρα ‘horns’, and ἐκ κεφαλῆς is ‘from the head’. ἑκκαιδεκάδωρα is ‘sixteen-palm-long’, made on δῶρον in its rarer sense ‘palm’, a hand’s breadth, which is a different word from δῶρον ‘gift’ in 97. πεφύκει is a pluperfect of φύω ‘grow’: ‘had grown’, with the growth seen as long finished.

sentences.t: καὶ τὰ μὲν ἀσκήσας κεραοξόος ἤραρε τέκτων,
sentences.l: and these, having worked them, a horn-polishing craftsman fitted together,
sentences.i: and a craftsman who polishes horn worked them and fitted them together,
sentences.n: Now the bow is made. τὰ μέν ‘these’ are the horns of 109, the object of ἤραρε, an aorist of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit, join’. κεραοξόος is a compound of κέρας ‘horn’ and the root of ξέω ‘scrape smooth, polish’, so ‘horn-polishing’; τέκτων is a skilled craftsman. ἀσκήσας ‘having worked’ is an aorist participle of ἀσκέω ‘work with skill’. The horns are the arms of the bow, which the craftsman joins into one piece.

sentences.t: πᾶν δ’ εὖ λειήνας χρυσέην ἐπέθηκε κορώνην.
sentences.l: and all of it well smoothed, a golden tip he put on.
sentences.i: and when he had smoothed it all well he fitted a golden tip on it.
sentences.n: πᾶν ‘all of it’ is the whole bow, object of λειήνας, the aorist participle of λειαίνω ‘make smooth’. κορώνη, literally ‘crow’, also means anything curved like a beak; here the usual explanation is the curved end-piece of the bow, and ‘tip’ is the plain word for it. χρυσέην is ‘golden’. ἐπέθηκε is the aorist of ἐπιτίθημι ‘put on’, and the subject is still the craftsman.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν εὖ κατέθηκε τανυσσάμενος ποτὶ γαίῃ
ἀγκλίνας·
sentences.l:
And this he set down well, having stretched it, against the ground,
leaning it;
sentences.i: And he strung it and set it carefully down, leaning it against the ground;
sentences.n: Now Pandarus himself acts again. τὸ μέν ‘this’ is the bow. τανυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of τανύω ‘stretch’, which of a bow means ‘string’: ‘having stretched it’ in the literal line, ‘strung’ in the English. εὖ is ‘well, carefully’. ποτί is the epic form of πρός, so ποτὶ γαίῃ, with the dative, is ‘against the ground’, and ἀγκλίνας ‘leaning’ is an aorist participle of ἀνακλίνω. The high point ends the unit.

sentences.t:
πρόσθεν δὲ σάκεα σχέθον ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι
μὴ πρὶν ἀναΐξειαν ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
πρὶν βλῆσθαι Μενέλαον ἀρήϊον Ἀτρέος υἱόν.
sentences.l:
and in front the good companions held their shields,
lest the warlike sons of the Achaeans spring up
before Menelaus, warlike son of Atreus, was struck.
sentences.i: and in front of him his good companions held up their shields, so that the warlike sons of the Achaeans might not spring up until Menelaus, the warlike son of Atreus, was hit.
sentences.n: The companions screen Pandarus so that the Achaeans cannot rush him before he shoots. σάκεα is ‘shields’, σχέθον an aorist of ἔχω without augment, ‘held’; the subject is ἑταῖροι ‘companions’, with ἐσθλοί ‘good’. μὴ πρίν … πρὶν βλῆσθαι is ‘lest … before … be struck’ (‘until’ in the English): μή gives the purpose, and βλῆσθαι is the epic aorist infinitive passive of βάλλω. ἀναΐξειαν is an aorist optative, ‘spring up’. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is said of both the Achaeans and Menelaus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ σύλα πῶμα φαρέτρης, ἐκ δ’ ἕλετ’ ἰὸν
ἀβλῆτα πτερόεντα μελαινέων ἕρμ’ ὀδυνάων·
sentences.l:
But he took the lid off the quiver, and took out an arrow,
unshot, winged, the prop of black pains;
sentences.i: Then he took the lid off his quiver and drew out an arrow that had never been shot, a winged one, the prop of black pains;
sentences.n: σύλα is the same verb as ἐσύλα at 105, here ‘took off’, with πῶμα ‘lid’ as its object. ἐκ … ἕλετο is ‘took out’ with the preposition split off. ἀβλῆτα, from ἀ- and βάλλω, is ‘unshot’, and πτερόεντα ‘winged’ is the stock epithet of arrows as of words. ἕρμα ‘prop’ is what holds something fast; applied to ‘black pains’ it makes the arrow their support or source, and the exact sense is not certain. μελαινέων ὀδυνάων is the epic genitive plural.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἐπὶ νευρῇ κατεκόσμει πικρὸν ὀϊστόν,
sentences.l: and quickly on the string he was setting in order the bitter arrow,
sentences.i: and quickly he fitted the bitter arrow on the string,
sentences.n: νευρῇ is the dative of νευρή ‘bowstring’. κατεκόσμει is the imperfect of κατακοσμέω ‘set in order, arrange’, a verb of careful placing, so ‘fitted’ in the English; the imperfect shows the act in progress. πικρόν ‘bitter’ is the arrow’s epithet. ὀϊστός here and ἰός in 116 both mean ‘arrow’, and the poet uses them for variety, not for different kinds of arrow.

sentences.t:
εὔχετο δ’ Ἀπόλλωνι Λυκηγενέϊ κλυτοτόξῳ
ἀρνῶν πρωτογόνων ῥέξειν κλειτὴν ἑκατόμβην
οἴκαδε νοστήσας ἱερῆς εἰς ἄστυ Ζελείης.
sentences.l:
and he prayed to Apollo, Lycia-born, famed for the bow,
that of first-born lambs he would sacrifice a famous hecatomb
when he had come home to the city of sacred Zeleia.
sentences.i: And he prayed to Apollo, the Lycia-born, famed for the bow, that he would sacrifice a famous hecatomb of first-born lambs when he had come home to the city of sacred Zeleia.
sentences.n: These three lines repeat Athena’s words of 101–103, with the imperative εὔχεο turned into the imperfect εὔχετο ‘was praying’ and ‘you’ turned into ‘he’. Pandarus does just what he was told, and the poet shows it by repeating the words. The stock epithets are translated again: Λυκηγενέϊ (sense not certain, ‘Lycia-born’ the usual explanation) and κλυτοτόξῳ ‘famed for the bow’. ῥέξειν is a future infinitive, ‘would sacrifice’.

sentences.t: ἕλκε δ’ ὁμοῦ γλυφίδας τε λαβὼν καὶ νεῦρα βόεια·
sentences.l: He drew back together, having taken hold, the notches and the ox-sinews;
sentences.i: He took hold of the nock and the ox-sinew string together and drew them back;
sentences.n: ἕλκε is the imperfect of ἕλκω ‘draw’, without augment, so ‘he drew back’ with the pull in progress. γλυφίδας are the notches cut in the end of the arrow for the string to sit in (the plural covers the one notch), and νεῦρα βόεια ‘ox-sinews’ is the bowstring, again a plural for one string. λαβών ‘having taken hold’ is the participle that carries the grip, and ὁμοῦ ‘together’ says he gripped notch and string in one pull.

sentences.t: νευρὴν μὲν μαζῷ πέλασεν, τόξῳ δὲ σίδηρον.
sentences.l: The string to his breast he brought near, and to the bow the iron.
sentences.i: He brought the string to his breast and the iron to the bow.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the two ends of the draw against each other. νευρήν ‘string’ is pulled back to μαζῷ ‘the breast’ (dative of the place it is brought to); σίδηρον ‘iron’ stands for the iron arrowhead, which comes back to the bow itself. πέλασεν is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, and its one verb serves both halves of the line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ κυκλοτερὲς μέγα τόξον ἔτεινε,
sentences.l: But when he had stretched the great bow into a circle,
sentences.i: And when he had drawn the great bow into a circle,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δή ‘but when indeed’ marks the moment just before the release. κυκλοτερές ‘rounded, in a circle’ is an adverb here, saying how far the bow is bent; μέγα τόξον is ‘the great bow’, and ἔτεινε ‘stretched’ is the aorist of τείνω. The main verbs, the sounds of the shot, come in the next unit.

sentences.t:
λίγξε βιός, νευρὴ δὲ μέγ’ ἴαχεν, ἆλτο δ’ ὀϊστὸς
ὀξυβελὴς καθ’ ὅμιλον ἐπιπτέσθαι μενεαίνων.
sentences.l:
The bow twanged, and the string cried out loudly, and leapt the arrow,
sharp-shafted, eager to fly onward through the throng.
sentences.i: The bow twanged and the string rang out loudly, and the sharp-pointed arrow leapt, eager to fly onward through the throng.
sentences.n: The shot: two sounds and one movement. λίγξε is an aorist ‘twanged’; βιός is the bow (the accent tells it from βίος ‘life’), and νευρή ‘string’ is the subject of ἴαχεν ‘cried out’, so both parts of the weapon are heard. ἆλτο, from ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, is an aorist; ὀξυβελής ‘sharp-shafted’ (‘sharp-pointed’ in the English) describes the arrow. ἐπιπτέσθαι is an infinitive of ἐπιπέτομαι ‘fly at, fly on’, here ‘fly onward’, and it goes with μενεαίνων ‘eager’; καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the crowd’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ σέθεν Μενέλαε θεοὶ μάκαρες λελάθοντο
ἀθάνατοι,
sentences.l:
Nor of you, Menelaus, did the blessed gods forget,
the immortal ones,
sentences.i: And the blessed gods did not forget you, Menelaus, the immortal ones,
sentences.n: The narrator turns to speak to Menelaus himself, with the vocative Μενέλαε. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ ‘you’, and λελάθοντο, the aorist middle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, takes the genitive. θεοὶ μάκαρες … ἀθάνατοι ‘blessed gods, immortal ones’ is a stock phrase; its second adjective is carried over into the first word of 128, with a comma, before the one god who matters is brought in.

sentences.t:
πρώτη δὲ Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἀγελείη,
ἥ τοι πρόσθε στᾶσα βέλος ἐχεπευκὲς ἄμυνεν.
sentences.l:
and first the daughter of Zeus, the spoil-driver,
who, standing in front, warded off the sharp-pointed shaft.
sentences.i: and first of all the daughter of Zeus, the driver of spoil, who stood in front and warded off the sharp shaft.
sentences.n: Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἀγελείη is Athena, not named: ‘the daughter of Zeus, the spoil-driver’. ἀγελείη is probably ἄγω ‘drive’ + λεία ‘spoil’, but the sense is not certain. πρώτη ‘first’ puts her ahead of the other gods in guarding him. στᾶσα is an aorist participle ‘having stood’, πρόσθε ‘in front’, and ἄμυνεν ‘warded off’ is the imperfect of ἀμύνω. βέλος ἐχεπευκές is ‘the sharp-pointed shaft’, ‘sharp shaft’ in the English (ἐχεπευκής, formation uncertain). Athena, who sent Pandarus to shoot, now turns the arrow.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ τόσον μὲν ἔεργεν ἀπὸ χροὸς ὡς ὅτε μήτηρ
παιδὸς ἐέργῃ μυῖαν ὅθ’ ἡδέϊ λέξεται ὕπνῳ,
sentences.l:
And she kept it off from his skin only so far as when a mother
keeps a fly from her child when he lies down in sweet sleep,
sentences.i: She kept it away from his skin only as far as a mother keeps a fly off her child when he lies down in sweet sleep,
sentences.n: A small comparison, about how little the goddess did: she only turned the arrow, as a mother only brushes off a fly. τόσον … ὡς ὅτε is ‘so far … as when’. ἔεργεν and ἐέργῃ are forms of εἴργω ‘keep off’ (imperfect, then the subjunctive of the general comparison); ἀπὸ χροός is ‘from the skin’. λέξεται is from λέχομαι ‘lie down to rest’, a different verb from λέγω ‘say’. The point is that the arrow was deflected, not stopped.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δ’ αὖτ’ ἴθυνεν ὅθι ζωστῆρος ὀχῆες
χρύσειοι σύνεχον καὶ διπλόος ἤντετο θώρηξ.
sentences.l:
And herself in turn she guided it to where of the belt the golden clasps
held together and the double breastplate met them.
sentences.i: And she herself guided it to the place where the golden clasps of the belt held fast and the double breastplate met them.
sentences.n: αὐτὴ δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and she herself, in turn’: Athena, having kept the arrow from the skin, now steers it. ἴθυνεν is the aorist of ἰθύνω ‘make straight, steer’. ὀχῆες are the fastenings of the belt, ζωστῆρος ‘belt’ being the broad belt worn at the waist, and σύνεχον ‘held together’ is an imperfect. διπλόος ‘double’ describes the breastplate, and ἤντετο, from ἀντάω, is ‘met’; the Greek does not say what it met, and ‘them’, the clasps, is supplied.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἔπεσε ζωστῆρι ἀρηρότι πικρὸς ὀϊστός·
sentences.l: and into the fitted belt fell the bitter arrow;
sentences.i: and the bitter arrow fell into the close-fitting belt;
sentences.n: ἐν … ἔπεσε is ‘fell in’, with the preposition split from its verb. ζωστῆρι ἀρηρότι is a dative: ἀρηρότι is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, so a belt that fits close, with no gap. The line begins the list of what the arrow passed through: the belt here, then the breastplate and the belly-guard in the lines that follow.

sentences.t: διὰ μὲν ἂρ ζωστῆρος ἐλήλατο δαιδαλέοιο,
sentences.l: Through the belt it had been driven, the wrought one,
sentences.i: It was driven through the finely wrought belt,
sentences.n: διὰ … ἐλήλατο is ‘it was driven through’: ἐλήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, with the arrow as the subject. ζωστῆρος is the genitive after διά, and δαιδαλέοιο is its epic ending; δαιδαλέος ‘wrought’ (‘finely wrought’ in the English) comes from the same root as δαίδαλον, a thing made with skill. μὲν ἄρ ‘indeed then’ opens a series that continues with καὶ διὰ …

sentences.t:
καὶ διὰ θώρηκος πολυδαιδάλου ἠρήρειστο
μίτρης θ’, ἣν ἐφόρει ἔρυμα χροὸς ἕρκος ἀκόντων,
sentences.l:
and through the much-wrought breastplate it was driven
and (through) the belly-guard, which he wore as protection for his skin, a fence against javelins,
sentences.i: and it was driven through the richly wrought breastplate as well, and through the belly-guard, which he wore as protection for his skin, a bulwark against javelins,
sentences.n: The first line has the same words as 3.358. ἠρήρειστο is the pluperfect passive of ἐρείδω ‘press, drive’, with the arrow as subject again; πολυδαιδάλου is ‘much-wrought’. μίτρης is the genitive of μίτρη (after the same διά), the usual explanation being a metal guard for the lower belly, worn under the belt, so ‘belly-guard’. ἔρυμα ‘protection’ and ἕρκος ‘fence’ say what it was for, with no linking word, and ἀκόντων is ‘javelins’.

sentences.t: ἥ οἱ πλεῖστον ἔρυτο· διὰ πρὸ δὲ εἴσατο καὶ τῆς.
sentences.l: which for him protected most; and clean through, it sped, even through this one.
sentences.i: which protected him most; but the arrow sped straight through that as well.
sentences.n: ἥ ‘which’ is the belly-guard, οἱ ‘for him’, πλεῖστον ‘most’, and ἔρυτο ‘protected’ is a form of ἔρυμαι, the verb that ἔρυμα in the line before is built on. διὰ πρό is two words with the force of ‘right through’, and εἴσατο is an aorist of ἵεμαι ‘rush, speed’; the subject is the arrow. καὶ τῆς ‘even through this one’ makes the guard the last and best defence, passed like the others.

sentences.t: ἀκρότατον δ’ ἄρ’ ὀϊστὸς ἐπέγραψε χρόα φωτός·
sentences.l: and the topmost skin of the man the arrow grazed;
sentences.i: and the arrow grazed the very surface of the man’s skin;
sentences.n: ἐπέγραψε is the aorist of ἐπιγράφω ‘scratch on the surface’, so ‘grazed’, and ἀκρότατον is the superlative of ἄκρος ‘top’: the arrow broke only the outermost skin. χρόα is the accusative of χρώς ‘skin, flesh’, and φωτός ‘of the man’ is Menelaus, from φώς ‘man’. After three layers of armour, the wound proves shallow, and the poet moves on at once to the blood.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἔρρεεν αἷμα κελαινεφὲς ἐξ ὠτειλῆς.
sentences.l: and at once there flowed blood, dark-clouded, from the wound.
sentences.i: and at once blood dark as a cloud flowed from the wound.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα δ’ ‘and at once’ links the graze to its result. ἔρρεεν is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’, with the doubled ρ left by the augment, so ‘was flowing’. κελαινεφές ‘dark-clouded’ is the word used of Zeus in other lines; applied to blood it is ‘dark as a cloud’ in the English, as in the Odyssey. ὠτειλή is a wound, here the cut the arrow made; ἐξ ὠτειλῆς is ‘from the wound’, and αἷμα ‘blood’ is the subject.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τίς τ’ ἐλέφαντα γυνὴ φοίνικι μιήνῃ
Μῃονὶς ἠὲ Κάειρα παρήϊον ἔμμεναι ἵππων·
sentences.l:
And as when some woman stains ivory with crimson,
a Maeonian or a Carian woman, to be a cheek-piece for horses;
sentences.i: Just as when a Maeonian or Carian woman stains ivory with crimson to make a cheek-piece for horses;
sentences.n: A comparison begins, picturing the blood on Menelaus’ pale skin as dye on ivory. ὡς δ’ ὅτε … τίς τ’ is ‘as when some …’, a general ‘some woman’. φοίνικι is ‘with crimson’ (the red-purple dye) and μιήνῃ is a subjunctive of μιαίνω ‘stain’. Μῃονίς is a woman of Maeonia (Lydia), Κάειρα of Caria, two regions of Asia Minor. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to be’, giving the purpose, and παρήϊον is a cheek-piece of a horse’s bridle.

sentences.t:
κεῖται δ’ ἐν θαλάμῳ, πολέες τέ μιν ἠρήσαντο
ἱππῆες φορέειν·
sentences.l:
and it lies in a chamber, and many horsemen have prayed
to carry it;
sentences.i: and it lies in a chamber, and many horsemen have prayed to carry it;
sentences.n: A θάλαμος is a chamber, an inner room where valuables are kept, and the object lies there unused. κεῖται ‘lies’ is the present of κεῖμαι, as of a thing stored. ἠρήσαντο is an aorist of ἀράομαι ‘pray, wish for’, with the infinitive φορέειν ‘to carry, to wear’ giving the wish; the ἱππῆες ‘horsemen’ want it but do not get it. The high point after φορέειν ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t:
βασιλῆϊ δὲ κεῖται ἄγαλμα,
ἀμφότερον κόσμός θ’ ἵππῳ ἐλατῆρί τε κῦδος·
sentences.l:
but for a king it lies as a treasure,
both an ornament for the horse and for the driver a glory;
sentences.i: but it lies there as a treasure for a king, both an ornament for his horse and a glory for the man who drives it;
sentences.n: βασιλῆϊ is the epic dative of βασιλεύς ‘king’. ἄγαλμα is a thing of pleasure or pride; the Odyssey renders it ‘a glory’, but κῦδος ‘glory’ stands in the next line, so ‘treasure’ here. ἀμφότερον, neuter, ‘both’, sums up the two uses that follow: κόσμος ‘ornament’ for the horse (ἵππῳ), κῦδος ‘glory’ for the ἐλατήρ ‘driver’, from ἐλαύνω ‘drive’.

sentences.t:
τοῖοί τοι Μενέλαε μιάνθην αἵματι μηροὶ
εὐφυέες κνῆμαί τε ἰδὲ σφυρὰ κάλ’ ὑπένερθε.
sentences.l:
Of such sort, Menelaus, were stained with blood your thighs,
shapely, and your shins and the fair ankles beneath.
sentences.i: Just so, Menelaus, were your shapely thighs stained with blood, and your shins and the fair ankles below.
sentences.n: The comparison closes: τοῖοι ‘of such a kind’ answers ὡς in 141, and the narrator again speaks to Menelaus (Μενέλαε). τοι is the enclitic dative of σύ, ‘to you’, turned into ‘your’ in the English. μιάνθην is a third-person plural aorist passive of μιαίνω ‘stain’, without augment, the verb of μιήνῃ in 141, so dye and blood are one word. εὐφυέες ‘shapely’ goes with μηροί ‘thighs’; κνῆμαι ‘shins’ and σφυρά ‘ankles’ are the lower leg, and ὑπένερθε ‘below’ ends the line.

sentences.t:
ῥίγησεν δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
ὡς εἶδεν μέλαν αἷμα καταρρέον ἐξ ὠτειλῆς·
sentences.l:
And he shuddered then, the lord of men, Agamemnon,
when he saw the black blood flowing down from the wound;
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, shuddered when he saw the black blood running down from the wound;
sentences.n: The narration turns to the watching Achaeans. ῥίγησεν is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, here with fear, as the next lines show; ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock epithet. ὡς εἶδεν is ‘when he saw’. μέλαν αἷμα ‘black blood’ recalls αἷμα κελαινεφές in 140, and καταρρέον is a participle ‘flowing down’.

sentences.t: ῥίγησεν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος.
sentences.l: And he shuddered too himself, Ares-loved Menelaus.
sentences.i: And Menelaus, dear to Ares, shuddered too.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘himself’ with καί ‘too’ sets Menelaus beside his brother: the wounded man shudders as well. The verb ῥίγησεν begins the line as it began 148, one word for both brothers. ἀρηΐφιλος ‘Ares-loved’ is a stock epithet, translated every time as ‘dear to Ares’ in the English.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ ἴδεν νεῦρόν τε καὶ ὄγκους ἐκτὸς ἐόντας
ἄψορρόν οἱ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀγέρθη.
sentences.l:
But when he saw the sinew and the barbs being outside,
back again for him the heart in his chest was gathered.
sentences.i: But when he saw that the sinew and the barbs were outside, his heart came back together in his chest.
sentences.n: The subject is now Menelaus: οἱ ‘for him’ is the one who looked. νεῦρον ‘sinew’ here is probably the binding that held the arrowhead to the shaft, and ὄγκοι ‘barbs’ are the hooks of the head; seeing both ἐκτὸς ἐόντας ‘being outside’ tells him the arrow has not gone deep. ἄψορρον ‘back again’ and ἀγέρθη, the aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, describe the θυμός ‘heart’ pulling itself together.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δὲ βαρὺ στενάχων μετέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
χειρὸς ἔχων Μενέλαον, ἐπεστενάχοντο δ’ ἑταῖροι·
sentences.l:
And among them, groaning heavily, spoke lord Agamemnon,
holding Menelaus by the hand, and the companions groaned along:
sentences.i: And among them lord Agamemnon spoke, groaning heavily, holding Menelaus by the hand, and the companions joined in his groaning:
sentences.n: This is the introduction of Agamemnon’s speech. τοῖς δέ ‘and among them’ is the dative of the listeners, and μετέφη ‘spoke among’ is the aorist of μεταφημί. βαρὺ στενάχων ‘groaning heavily’ and κρείων ‘lord’ (here with Ἀγαμέμνων) are stock phrases. χειρὸς ἔχων is ‘holding by the hand’, the genitive of the part held. ἐπεστενάχοντο is the imperfect of ἐπιστενάχομαι ‘groan in addition’: the companions take up his groan.

sentences.t:
φίλε κασίγνητε θάνατόν νύ τοι ὅρκι’ ἔταμνον
οἶον προστήσας πρὸ Ἀχαιῶν Τρωσὶ μάχεσθαι,
sentences.l:
“Dear brother, death indeed for you the oaths I was cutting,
setting you alone forward before the Achaeans to fight the Trojans,
sentences.i: “Dear brother, it was your death that I was making the oaths for, when I set you out alone before the Achaeans to fight the Trojans,
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s grief begins as self-reproach. ὅρκι’ ἔταμνον ‘I was cutting oaths’ means making a treaty: the verb τάμνω ‘cut’ recalls the cutting of the victims at an oath-sacrifice. θάνατον … τοι ‘death for you’ is what the oaths turned out to be. προστήσας, an aorist participle of προΐστημι, is ‘having set forward’, and οἶον ‘alone’ is Menelaus, the single champion who stepped out for the duel of book 3. νύ is ‘now, indeed’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of φίλε is lengthened for the long of the first foot, and the short final syllable of κασίγνητε must count long in the third foot.

sentences.t: ὥς σ’ ἔβαλον Τρῶες, κατὰ δ’ ὅρκια πιστὰ πάτησαν.
sentences.l: so the Trojans have struck you, and trampled down the faithful oaths.
sentences.i: And so the Trojans have hit you and trampled down the faithful oaths.
sentences.n: ὥς σ’ may be ὡς + σε, the accent falling on ὡς only because the enclitic follows; it is read ‘so, thus’, pointing back to what Agamemnon has just said, and could also be ‘since’. ἔβαλον is the aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’; κατὰ … πάτησαν is καταπατέω with the preposition split off, ‘trampled down’. ὅρκια πιστά ‘faithful oaths’ is the standing phrase for the sworn truce of book 3.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν πως ἅλιον πέλει ὅρκιον αἷμά τε ἀρνῶν
σπονδαί τ’ ἄκρητοι καὶ δεξιαὶ ᾗς ἐπέπιθμεν.
sentences.l:
Not at all in any way vain is the oath, and the blood of the lambs,
and the unmixed libations, and the right hands in which we trusted.
sentences.i: No, the oath is not vain, nor the blood of the lambs, the unmixed libations, and the right hands in which we trusted.
sentences.n: οὐ μέν πως is ‘surely not in any way’, and ἅλιον ‘vain’ is the word of 26 in the last part. One adjective and one singular verb (πέλει) cover four subjects, all parts of the oath ritual: ὅρκιον ‘oath’, the blood of the lambs, the σπονδαί ‘libations’, ἄκρητοι ‘unmixed’ (no water added), and the δεξιαί ‘right hands’ clasped as a pledge. ᾗς ἐπέπιθμεν is ‘in which we trusted’: ᾗς is the epic dative plural of the relative, and ἐπέπιθμεν is the pluperfect of πέποιθα (πείθομαι) used for ‘we trusted’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ τε καὶ αὐτίκ’ Ὀλύμπιος οὐκ ἐτέλεσσεν,
ἔκ τε καὶ ὀψὲ τελεῖ,
sentences.l:
For even if the Olympian did not fulfil it at once,
yet even late he fulfils it,
sentences.i: For even if the Olympian has not fulfilled it at once, he fulfils it late all the same,
sentences.n: A general truth about gods and oaths. εἴ περ … καί is ‘even if’, with γάρ ‘for’ tying it to the last unit and the τε of general statements. Ὀλύμπιος ‘the Olympian’ is Zeus, who watches over oaths, unnamed. ἐτέλεσσεν is the aorist of τελέω ‘fulfil’; its object, the punishment of oath-breakers, is left unsaid. ἔκ τε … τελεῖ is ‘he fulfils out’, ἐκτελέω with the preposition split off, and the present tense states what is always so; ὀψέ is ‘late’.

sentences.t:
σύν τε μεγάλῳ ἀπέτισαν
σὺν σφῇσιν κεφαλῇσι γυναιξί τε καὶ τεκέεσσιν.
sentences.l:
and with a great one they paid back,
with their own heads, with wives and with children.
sentences.i: and they pay at great cost, with their own heads, and with their wives and children.
sentences.n: The subject, those who broke the oath, is not stated. ἀπέτισαν is a gnomic aorist of ἀποτίνω ‘pay back’, an aorist that says what regularly happens, hence ‘they pay’ in the English. σὺν μεγάλῳ has no noun, ‘with a great (one)’, and the English supplies only ‘cost’. σύν is repeated, ‘with their own heads, with wives and children’, so the price is their lives and their families. σφῇσιν is the epic dative plural of σφός ‘their own’.

sentences.t: εὖ γὰρ ἐγὼ τόδε οἶδα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.l: for well I know this in mind and in heart:
sentences.i: For I know this well, in my mind and heart:
sentences.n: This line stands in the Odyssey too, and its English is the same here. εὖ γάρ ‘for well’ gives the ground of what Agamemnon is about to say: he knows it for certain. οἶδα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I know’. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’ is a formula for knowing inwardly, φρήν being the thinking part and θυμός the feeling one. The colon opens the prophecy.

sentences.t:
ἔσσεται ἦμαρ ὅτ’ ἄν ποτ’ ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἱρὴ
καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο,
sentences.l:
there will be a day when at some time shall have perished sacred Ilium
and Priam and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear,
sentences.i: There will come a day when sacred Ilium will have perished, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear,
sentences.n: The day of Troy’s fall, stated as certain. ὅτ’ ἄν ποτ’ is ‘when at some time’, with the subjunctive ὀλώλῃ, the perfect of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, ‘shall have perished’, so the ruin is seen as complete. The three subjects are Ἴλιος ἱρή ‘sacred Ilium’, Πρίαμος and the λαός of Priam, whose stock epithet ἐϋμμελίω is ‘of the good ash-spear’. These are Zeus’s own words about the city he loved best (4.46–47 in the last part), now in Agamemnon’s mouth as a prophecy.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δέ σφι Κρονίδης ὑψίζυγος αἰθέρι ναίων
αὐτὸς ἐπισσείῃσιν ἐρεμνὴν αἰγίδα πᾶσι
τῆσδ’ ἀπάτης κοτέων·
sentences.i: and Zeus, the son of Cronus, who sits on high and dwells in the bright upper air, himself shall shake the dusky aegis over them all, in resentment at this deceit;
sentences.n: The ‘when’ of 164 goes on: ‘a day when Ilium shall perish … and Zeus shall shake’. ἐπισσείῃσιν is a present subjunctive with the old ending -σιν, and σφι is ‘over them’, the Trojans. The aegis is what Zeus shakes to bring terror; ἐρεμνήν is ‘dusky’. ὑψίζυγος ‘sitting on high’ is explained from ὕψι ‘high’ and ζυγόν ‘bench, seat’, but its exact sense is not certain; αἰθέρι ναίων is the formula ‘dwelling in the aether’. τῆσδ’ ἀπάτης κοτέων is ‘bearing a grudge over this deceit’, the deceit being the broken oath.

sentences.t: τὰ μὲν ἔσσεται οὐκ ἀτέλεστα·
sentences.l: these things will not be unaccomplished;
sentences.i: and these things will not go unaccomplished;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν ‘these things’ looks back on the whole prophecy. ἀτέλεστα ‘unaccomplished’ is the adjective of 26 and 57 in the last part, where Hera used it for her labour. The double negative οὐκ ἀτέλεστα makes the claim strong: the prophecy will be accomplished. The colon makes a stop before the personal turn of ἀλλά in 169.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι αἰνὸν ἄχος σέθεν ἔσσεται ὦ Μενέλαε
αἴ κε θάνῃς καὶ πότμον ἀναπλήσῃς βιότοιο.
sentences.l:
But for me fearsome grief for you there will be, Menelaus,
if you die and fill up the doom of your life.
sentences.i: But I shall feel fearsome grief for you, Menelaus, if you die and fill up the doom of your life.
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the turn from the fate of Troy to Agamemnon’s own fear. μοι ‘for me’ and σέθεν ‘for you, on your account’ (genitive) frame αἰνὸν ἄχος ‘fearsome grief’, and ἔσσεται is ‘will be’. αἴ κε θάνῃς is the epic form of εἰ κε with an aorist subjunctive, ‘if you die’. ἀναπλήσῃς is ‘fill up’, and πότμον βιότοιο ‘the doom of life’ pictures death as completing the measure of a life.

sentences.t: καί κεν ἐλέγχιστος πολυδίψιον Ἄργος ἱκοίμην·
sentences.l: And I should come, most shameful, to much-thirsty Argos;
sentences.i: And I should come, most shameful, to very thirsty Argos;
sentences.n: καί κεν … ἱκοίμην is a potential optative, ‘I should come’, a picture of Agamemnon’s return if Menelaus dies. ἐλέγχιστος ‘most shameful’ is the superlative of ἐλεγχής ‘shameful’; Odysseus used the same word of Agamemnon at 2.285. πολυδίψιον is ‘much-thirsty’, a name for Argos as dry land. Ἄργος is Argos, the land of the two brothers.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα γὰρ μνήσονται Ἀχαιοὶ πατρίδος αἴης·
sentences.l: for at once the Achaeans will remember their fatherland;
sentences.i: for the Achaeans will at once remember their fatherland;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα γάρ ‘for at once’ gives the reason: the army will lose heart as soon as Menelaus dies. μνήσονται is the future middle of μιμνήσκομαι with the genitive, ‘will remember’, and it carries the sense ‘will turn their minds to going home’. πατρίδος αἴης ‘fatherland’ is the epic phrase that elsewhere has φίλη ‘dear’ with it.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δέ κεν εὐχωλὴν Πριάμῳ καὶ Τρωσὶ λίποιμεν
Ἀργείην Ἑλένην·
sentences.l:
and we should leave behind as a boast for Priam and the Trojans
Argive Helen;
sentences.i: and we should leave Argive Helen behind as a boast for Priam and the Trojans;
sentences.n: κὰδ … λίποιμεν is καταλείπω with the preposition split off (κὰδ because the τ of κατά becomes δ before the δ of δέ), ‘leave behind’, an optative with κεν that carries on the picture of defeat. εὐχωλήν ‘a boast’ is something to boast of, as at 2.160: Helen would be left to the Trojans as proof of their victory. Ἀργείην Ἑλένην ‘Argive Helen’ is her usual title, and the high point ends the unit. The ‘we’ includes Agamemnon himself.

sentences.t:
σέο δ’ ὀστέα πύσει ἄρουρα
κειμένου ἐν Τροίῃ ἀτελευτήτῳ ἐπὶ ἔργῳ.
sentences.l:
and your bones the plough-land will rot,
as you lie in Troy upon an unfulfilled task.
sentences.i: and the plough-land will rot your bones as you lie in Troy with the task unfulfilled.
sentences.n: σέο is the epic genitive of σύ ‘you’; it goes with ὀστέα ‘bones’ and with κειμένου ‘lying’, which agrees with it. πύσει is the future of πύθω ‘rot’. ἄρουρα ‘plough-land’ is the soil that will cover him. ἀτελευτήτῳ ἐπὶ ἔργῳ ‘over a task unfulfilled’ says the war has not been won: the matter for which Menelaus died stays undone. ἀτελεύτητος ‘unfulfilled’ is a rarer word than ἀτέλεστος ‘unaccomplished’.

sentences.t:
καί κέ τις ὧδ’ ἐρέει Τρώων ὑπερηνορεόντων
τύμβῳ ἐπιθρῴσκων Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο·
sentences.l:
And someone will say thus, of the over-bold Trojans,
leaping upon the tomb of Menelaus the glorious:
sentences.i: And one of the overbearing Trojans will say, as he leaps upon the tomb of glorious Menelaus:
sentences.n: Agamemnon imagines a scene. καί κέ τις … ἐρέει is ‘and someone will say’, ἐρέει being a future of εἶπον, and Τρώων ὑπερηνορεόντων ‘of the over-bold Trojans’ says which group he comes from; ὑπερηνορέω is built on ὑπέρ and ἠνορέη ‘manliness’. ἐπιθρῴσκων ‘leaping upon’ puts the Trojan on Menelaus’ τύμβῳ ‘tomb’. κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet, used here of the dead man. The colon opens the imagined speech.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ οὕτως ἐπὶ πᾶσι χόλον τελέσει’ Ἀγαμέμνων,
ὡς καὶ νῦν ἅλιον στρατὸν ἤγαγεν ἐνθάδ’ Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l:
‘Would that Agamemnon might thus fulfil his anger on all,
as now too he has led here a vain army of Achaeans,
sentences.i: ‘If only Agamemnon would fulfil his anger on everyone, just as he has now led the army of the Achaeans here in vain,
sentences.n: The imagined Trojan’s speech begins with a wish. αἴθ’ ‘would that’ takes an optative, τελέσει’ for τελέσειε, ‘might he fulfil’. χόλον τελέσει’ ‘fulfil his anger’ is to act it out. ἐπὶ πᾶσι ‘on all’ may mean all the Achaeans or all men. ὡς καὶ νῦν ‘as even now’ points to the failed expedition: ἅλιον ‘vain’ goes with στρατόν ‘army’, ἤγαγεν is ‘led’, and ἐνθάδ’ is ‘here’. The sneer is that this is what Agamemnon’s anger has brought.
sentences.mark: A Trojan speaks, as Agamemnon imagines it

sentences.t:
καὶ δὴ ἔβη οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
σὺν κεινῇσιν νηυσὶ λιπὼν ἀγαθὸν Μενέλαον.
sentences.l:
and indeed he has gone home to his dear fatherland
with empty ships, leaving behind good Menelaus.’
sentences.i: and now he has gone home to his dear fatherland with empty ships, leaving good Menelaus behind.’
sentences.n: The taunt goes on. καὶ δὴ ἔβη ‘and indeed he has gone’ uses the aorist for a finished act. οἶκον δέ, printed as two words, is ‘homewards’, and ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘to the fatherland’ repeats the direction, with φίλην ‘dear’. κεινῇσιν is the epic dative of κενός ‘empty’: the ships carry home no spoil. λιπών ‘leaving’ is an aorist participle, and ἀγαθόν ‘good’ is the epithet the Trojan gives the dead man.

sentences.t: ὥς ποτέ τις ἐρέει· τότε μοι χάνοι εὐρεῖα χθών.
sentences.l: So someday someone will say; then for me may the wide earth gape.”
sentences.i: That is what someone will say one day; and then may the wide earth open for me.”
sentences.n: ὥς ‘so’ closes the imagined speech, and ποτέ ‘some day’ puts it in the future; ἐρέει is the same future as in 176. The wish after the high point is Agamemnon’s own: τότε ‘then’, μοι ‘for me’, χάνοι (an optative of χάσκω ‘gape’), εὐρεῖα χθών ‘the wide earth’. It is a wish to be swallowed alive rather than hear the taunt. With this image of shame his speech, and the part, end.
